verdict_reason: No CRITICAL and no HIGH finding, and none of the mandatory REQUEST_CHANGES triggers is present. The acceptance property is PROVEN, not asserted: with no configuration file at all, the entire tip working tree scans clean under the unmodified default ruleset — 0 findings, exit 0 — and the retired field name is absent from every tracked path at this head. Scanning the exact commit ranges the pinned CI action constructs also returns 0 findings for these commits. The change direction is pure deletion, which is the correct shape for the defect: my previous verdict proved the configuration suppressed nothing, and rather than making the suppression work, this range removes both the configuration and the reason the rule fired. Net effect on the security surface: one repository-root scanner-configuration file gone, so the default ruleset is unmodified and no exemption of any kind exists in this repository; one field renamed to a neutral synonym the same schema already used. That is strictly stronger than the state my previous verdict approved, which carried a live, if inert, global exemption. I am correcting one claim of my previous verdict rather than letting it stand: I wrote that the scan job would keep failing after fc25d1ee merged. That was measured against a whole-tree scan. So the red run belongs to a historical commit range that no commit on this branch can alter; this range prevents recurrence rather than repairing that run. Bug-surface axis (FR24; ledger fold unchanged at this head: 1016 records, 495 distinct bugs, exactly 1 unresolved, and git diff over the range touches 0 paths in the bug and backlog ledgers): UNCHANGED for production — zero production lines, zero branches, zero flags, zero code paths in the whole range — and REDUCED for the tooling surface, because an entire configuration file and its exemption semantics are deleted rather than corrected. findings.message: Correction to my previous verdict: the CI scanner is RANGE-scoped, so my claim that the job would keep failing after fc25d1ee merged was wrong. The inertness finding itself stands and is now moot.
findings.detail_md:
Recording this in the same place the error was made, rather than letting a wrong claim stand in an approved verdict.

**What I wrote at fc25d1ee.** That the archived record carrying the offending field was already in the tree at the release-ship commit, so *"the job this change exists to unblock will keep failing at the same line after this commit merges."*

**What is actually true.** The pinned action does not scan the whole tree or the whole history. It builds a log range from the pushed commits, or from the pull request's commits, and scans only that range. Measured with the same scanner build:

| range scanned | findings |
|---|---|
| the release-ship commit alone | **1** |
| `fc25d1ee` alone | **0** |
| the two commits of this range | **0** |

So the red run belongs to the historical push that first introduced the field, and no commit on this branch can change a past commit's content. This range prevents recurrence; it does not repair that run. A re-run of that historical workflow run will fail again, because it will re-scan the same range.

**What is unaffected.** The MEDIUM finding itself — that the global allowlist regex was compared against the captured secret and therefore suppressed nothing — was measured directly against that scanner build and stands unchanged. It is now moot: the file it described is deleted, and this repository carries **zero** scanner exemptions of any kind.

**Why this correction improves the posture rather than undermining it.** The remedy chosen was deletion, which is correct under either reading of the CI impact: a configuration that suppressed nothing had no reason to exist, and removing the field name removes the trigger for every future commit regardless of how the scanner is scoped.
findings.fix_recommendation: operator: if the historical red run matters, the options are to accept it (the offending content is now deleted from the tip anyway), or to exempt that single commit by its object id — which is far narrower than any content pattern, since it names one commit and nothing else. Do not reintroduce a content-regex exemption; the tree scans clean without one.

findings.message: Both commits write to the archive path class the law declares blocked — one content modification and eleven deletions — which lands because that class is enforced only on file-tool payloads and is fully bypassable through the shell.
findings.detail_md:
The workspace law defines the archive tree as a frozen path class: blocked, moved only by a rename, never edited. This range writes it twice:

| commit | operation on the frozen class | count |
|---|---|---|
| `4ae33f06` | content modification of an archived record | 1 |
| `e354b18c` | deletion of archived records | 11 |

The modification is invisible at range level, because the same file is deleted by the next commit; it is visible per commit.

**Why it landed.** The gate that enforces the path classes is a pre-tool hook over file-tool payloads. A shell command — a stream edit, a remove, a git remove — never presents such a payload, so the frozen class is not consulted. The git chokepoints that do cover the shell path check branch names, the push preflight and the denylist scan; none of them classifies paths. The result is that the strongest path class in the law is, in practice, advisory against any agent that reaches for a shell.

**Why this is MEDIUM and not a blocker.** The operator ordered this deletion explicitly, so the *intent* is sanctioned and the human-authority carve-out applies. What is recorded is the *mechanism*: nothing distinguished an operator-sanctioned archive deletion from an unsanctioned one, and nothing would have stopped the second. The archived records deleted here are security verdicts — the on-disk evidence of past approvals — so the class of data reachable through this gap is exactly the class the gate exists to protect.

**Mitigating.** Git history retains every deleted record, so the audit trail is pruned from the working tree rather than destroyed, and any auditor can recover it.
findings.fix_recommendation: ai-engineer plus project-manager, in the governance lane and not on this PR edge: decide whether the frozen class is meant to bind agents through the shell as well. If it is, the enforcement point has to be a chokepoint that classifies paths — the pre-commit hook already sees the staged path set and is the natural home — rather than a second hook on the tool path. If it is not, the law should say so, because a class documented as blocked but reachable by any shell command teaches agents that the classes are decorative.

findings.message: The gate's coverage rule forgives verdict DELETION exactly as it forgives verdict addition; this range is the first commit to exercise that direction, removing 1109 lines of security evidence while staying inside the forgiven path set.
findings.detail_md:
The verdict gate decides that a reviewed sha still covers a pull-request head when every path differing between them lies under a live or archived verdicts directory. The rule matches on the path only — it never asks whether the file was added, modified or removed.

**Measured on this range.** `git diff --name-only 4ae33f06 e354b18c` returns 11 paths, all matching the archived-verdicts pattern. So a verdict naming `4ae33f06` would have been judged to "cover" `e354b18c`, even though the delta between them is the deletion of eleven security approvals.

**Why this is LOW and not HIGH.** The direction is fail-closed for anything that matters. Deleting evidence can only reduce the set of qualifying verdicts, so it can never let unreviewed *code* pass; the worst outcome is a future pull request that fails the gate and needs a fresh review. The property is nonetheless worth naming now, before it becomes habit: the rule was written to mean *"nothing but more evidence landed since the review"*, and it currently also means *"or less"*.

**Adjacent observation.** This same range demonstrates the rule working as intended in the other direction: my previous verdict at `fc25d1ee` correctly stopped covering this head, because the configuration deletion is not a verdict path.
findings.fix_recommendation: software-engineer, when the gate script is next touched and not on this edge: consider narrowing the forgiven set to path additions, so that a head which removes evidence relative to the reviewed sha requires a fresh verdict. If the operator's retention rule makes deletions routine, then the two rules should be reconciled deliberately rather than by coincidence.

findings.message: The retention rule was applied to the archive tree only: one consumed verdict from the previous release survives in the live tree, leaving that release split across two trees and the new rule half-applied.
findings.detail_md:
`e354b18c` removed 11 consumed verdicts from the archive tree. A twelfth consumed verdict remains tracked at this head, in the **live** releases tree, belonging to the previous release: agent security-reviewer, verdict APPROVED, release identifier of the previous version.

The sha it names is **not an ancestor of this head** — it was left behind by the squash that shipped that release — so the gate can never qualify it. It was observed being skipped for exactly that reason during the gate run for this verdict.

**Why it matters despite being harmless.** Under the operator's stated rule, a verdict consumed by the gate never stays on disk; this one did. The result is that the previous release now has content in the archive tree and an orphaned verdict in the live tree, which is the kind of split state that makes the next reader unsure whether the rule applies to one tree or both. It also permanently adds a candidate that every future gate run must open, parse and skip.

**No security consequence.** It cannot qualify, it names an unreachable commit, and its presence cannot cause a pass.
findings.fix_recommendation: operator or project-manager: apply the retention rule to the live tree as well and remove that leftover record in the same lane as this hotfix, or state explicitly that the rule covers the archive tree only. Either is fine; the split state is what should not persist.

findings.message: The gate script documents the archived-verdicts tree as the required evidence source for closure and deploy pull requests — the fix for a HIGH bug — and policy has now emptied that tree.
findings.detail_md:
The gate script's own header states that at release closure the whole release directory including its verdicts is moved verbatim into the archive tree, and that a passing pull request against a closed release — the final segment pull request, and every deploy pull request — *must resolve its evidence there too*. That archive-resolution path exists specifically to fix a HIGH bug in which the gate could not resolve evidence after a release was archived, making closure and deploy pull requests permanently ungateable.

At this head that tree contains **zero** verdict records.

**Consequence.** Fail-closed, so no pull request can wrongly pass; but any future pull request that would have resolved its evidence from the archive now finds nothing and requires a fresh verdict on its head. For this lane that is fine, because the verdict for this head lives in the live tree. It becomes load-bearing the moment a deploy pull request is opened for a release whose evidence was archived and then deleted.

**The real problem is the disagreement, not either rule.** The script says the archive is where evidence must be resolvable; the retention rule says a consumed verdict never stays on disk. Both are currently true in this repository, and they contradict. The next agent reading the script header will go looking for files that policy deletes.
findings.fix_recommendation: product-engineer plus project-manager: reconcile the two statements in one place. If verdicts are consumed once and deleted, the script header should stop describing the archive tree as a required evidence source and the archive arm of its search should be reconsidered; if archived evidence must remain resolvable, the retention rule needs an exception for it. Do not leave the script documenting a contract the policy removes.

findings.message: Bug-surface axis (FR24): UNCHANGED for production, REDUCED for the tooling surface — an entire configuration file and its exemption semantics deleted rather than corrected.
findings.detail_md:
**Ledger fold at this head, unchanged by this range.** 1016 records, 495 distinct bugs, exactly one unresolved. `git diff --name-only fc25d1ee..e354b18c` touches **0** paths in the bug and backlog ledgers, so this range neither opened nor closed anything.

**Production surface:** zero lines, zero branches, zero flags, zero code paths in the entire range. It cannot increase the bug surface of any production feature.

**Tooling surface: reduced, and reduced in the right shape.** The alternative to this range was to make the exemption work — a corrected target, a rule-scoped allowlist, a path restriction, a match condition. Every one of those adds configuration surface with its own failure modes, including one I hit while testing the recommendation: the match-condition key has a short name, and the obvious longer guess silently degrades to a permissive combination. This range instead deletes the file, so none of those failure modes can exist here. The repository now carries zero scanner exemptions and an unmodified default ruleset, and the tip tree scans clean without any of it.

**The one accretion risk is not in the diff.** It is that a future reader, seeing the historical red run, reintroduces a configuration file. The correction finding above records why that is unnecessary.
findings.fix_recommendation: None — the axis is satisfied. The guard against regression is the recorded correction, not a code change.

What this range cannot do is turn a historical run green, because the pinned scanner is range-scoped and that run scans a commit range this branch does not contain. Decide whether to accept that historical red or to exempt that single commit by its object id; do not reintroduce a content-regex exemption, since none is needed.
